analysis.one_liner: Replaces the graduated income tax with a single flat rate on wages and business income and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: The flat tax bill never got a hearing or a vote: after being sent to the tax-writing committee in March 1999, no action was taken on it for the rest of the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would throw out the current graduated income tax, where higher earners pay higher rates, and replace it with a single 19% rate (dropping to 17% after two years) on wages and business income. It would tax only cash wages, retirement payouts, and unemployment benefits — meaning money earned from investments (capital gains, dividends, interest) would not be taxed at all for individuals. It would also repeal the estate tax, the alternative minimum tax, all tax credits (including the Earned Income Tax Credit and child credit), and nearly all itemized deductions like mortgage interest and charitable giving.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy households and estates gain the most: investment income would go untaxed, the estate tax would disappear, and the top rate would fall from 39.6% to 17%. Businesses gain a lower, simpler tax (19% falling to 17%) replacing the corporate tax. Middle-income filers gain some relief from a much larger standard deduction and simpler filing.

how_it_helps.text: Sets a large standard deduction — $23,200 for joint filers, $11,600 for singles, plus $5,200 per dependent — so many families with modest wage income would owe nothing [S3].
Collapses the six-rate individual income tax (10% to 39.6%) into one 19% rate, dropping to 17% after two years [S2][S3].
Repeals the estate and gift taxes entirely, retroactive to deaths after December 31, 1998 [S2][S3].
Repeals the alternative minimum tax and all individual and business tax credits [S2][S3].
Dramatically simplifies filing: with only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment benefits taxable, most households would need only a postcard-sized return [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Households that rely on tax credits and deductions would pay more: the bill repeals the Earned Income Tax Credit, the child tax credit, and deductions for mortgage interest, charitable giving, and state and local taxes. Wage earners bear the entire individual income tax while investment income goes tax-free. The bill would also remove a large amount of federal revenue, forcing either deep spending cuts or larger deficits. Government agencies and nonprofits would owe a new 19% tax on the value of employee benefits like health insurance.
analysis.who_pays_short: Working families using credits and deductions

drawbacks.text: Repealing all credits ends the Earned Income Tax Credit and child credits, which are worth more to low- and moderate-income working families than the larger standard deduction gives back — many would see their taxes rise [S3].

Because only wages and a few benefits are taxable, capital gains, dividends, and interest income would escape individual tax entirely, shifting the overall tax burden toward people who earn by working [S3].
Repealing the estate and gift taxes entirely removes the only federal tax on large inherited wealth [S2][S3].
The bill repeals pension nondiscrimination and minimum-coverage rules, which currently prevent retirement plans from being designed to benefit only a company's highest-paid employees [S3].

Cutting both individual and business rates this deeply would remove far more revenue than it adds back, requiring large spending cuts or adding substantially to the federal debt (widely reported analysis of flat-tax proposals of this era).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The simplicity and the bigger standard deduction are real, and many middle-income families would file a simpler return and pay somewhat less. But the bill's net effect is a large upward transfer: investment income and estates would go untaxed while the credits and deductions that working families rely on disappear, and the revenue loss is large enough to force major cuts to public programs. An honest reading is that the family-friendly features are outweighed by the shift of the tax burden onto wages.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means Committee in March 1999 and the committee never took it up, so it simply sat there until the Congress ended two years later.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Armey, the House Majority Leader, introduced the flat tax bill on March 9, 1999, with five original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which writes tax law, and also to the Rules Committee [S1][S5].
The action history shows no further steps of any kind — no hearing, no mark-up, no committee vote, no floor action — through the end of the 106th Congress in January 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Low- and middle-income households that depend on the Earned Income Tax Credit and deductions like mortgage interest are better off that the bill died, since those provisions would have been repealed. No industry or household gained anything from the bill's failure; the existing tax code simply stayed in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Families who rely on tax credits and deductions

for.name: Rep. Richard K. Armey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the flat tax bill and led its promotion as his signature proposal.

for.name: 11 cosponsors (10 Republicans, 1 Democrat)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: The tax-writing committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or mark-up and never reported the bill to the floor during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call exists; its sponsorship was almost entirely Republican (10 of 11 cosponsors, plus a Republican lead sponsor), and the Republican-controlled tax committee let it die without action.

industries.note: The bill would eliminate tax on capital gains, dividends, and interest, cut the top rate by more than 20 points, and repeal the estate tax — the largest gains flowing to those with the most wealth. The revenue those taxes raise would otherwise fund government services or offset taxes on work.

industries.industry: Tax-exempt organizations and federal, state, and local government employers
industries.note: The bill would impose a new 19% tax on the value of noncash employee benefits (such as health insurance) provided by government agencies and nonprofits, raising the cost of employer-sponsored benefits for public-sector and nonprofit workers.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: A postcard-simple tax on wages would eliminate most of the demand for tax preparation and filing services. In this case the industry's loss would come alongside a genuine simplification benefit for taxpayers.

Repealing the mortgage interest deduction would weaken the tax incentive to buy homes, a change homebuilders and lenders have historically opposed. Consumers would lose the deduction too, so the industry's loss and the public's loss run together here.
Repealing the charitable deduction removes the main tax incentive for giving, which charities rely on for donations.
